A '''rational difference equation''' is a nonlinear [[difference equation]] of the form<ref>Skellam,  J.G. (1951).  “Random dispersal in theoretical populations”, ''Biometrika'' '''38''' 196−218, eqns (41,42)</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4Kb3lO31NcAC&q=on+third+order+rational+difference+equations|title=Dynamics of Third-Order Rational Difference Equations with Open Problems and Conjectures|first1=Elias|last1=Camouzis|first2=G.|last2=Ladas|date=November 16, 2007|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781584887669|via=Google Books}}</ref><ref name="Ladas-Kulenovic">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zW7N4r64aZgC&q=on+second+order+rational+difference+equations|title=Dynamics of Second Order Rational Difference Equations: With Open Problems and Conjectures|first1=Mustafa R. S.|last1=Kulenovic|first2=G.|last2=Ladas|date=July 30, 2001|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781420035384|via=Google Books}}</ref><ref>Newth, Gerald, "World order from chaotic beginnings", ''Mathematical Gazette'' 88, March 2004, 39-45 gives a trigonometric approach.</ref>
<math display="block">x_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha+\sum_{i=0}^k \beta_ix_{n-i}}{A+\sum_{i=0}^k B_ix_{n-i}}~,</math>
where the initial conditions <math>x_{0}, x_{-1},\dots, x_{-k}</math> are such that the denominator  never vanishes for any {{mvar|n}}.

==First-order rational difference equation==
A '''first-order rational difference equation''' is a nonlinear difference equation of the form

{{NumBlk|::|<math>w_{t+1} = \frac{aw_t+b}{cw_t+d}.</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

When <math>a,b,c,d</math> and the [[initial condition]] <math>w_0</math> are [[real number]]s, this difference equation is called a '''Riccati difference equation'''.<ref name="Ladas-Kulenovic"/>

Such an equation can be solved by writing <math>w_t</math> as a nonlinear transformation of another variable <math>x_t</math> which itself evolves linearly.  Then standard methods can be used to solve the [[linear difference equation]] in <math>x_t</math>.

Equations of this form arise from the infinite [[resistor ladder]] problem.<ref>{{cite web |title=Equivalent resistance in ladder circuit |url=https://physics.stackexchange.com/q/121297 |website=Stack Exchange |access-date=21 February 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Thinking Recursively: How to Crack the Infinite Resistor Ladder Puzzle! |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rqckorUt2ck |website=Youtube |access-date=21 February 2022}}</ref>

== Solving a first-order equation==

===First approach===

[[Without loss of generality|WLoG]], the determinant-like quantity <math>ad-bc\neq0</math>, and this can be easily seen by noting that, with a division on both the numerator and denominator in Equation {{EqNote|2}}, you can always set <math>c=1</math>, in which case, if <math>ad-bc=0</math>, then the numerator and denominator will cancel away, leaving no difference equation left, being instead so completely reduced as to become exactly the constant <math>a</math>. Thus, one approach<ref>Brand, Louis, "A sequence defined by a difference equation," ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'' '''62''', September 1955, 489&ndash;492.   [https://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2307362  online]</ref> to developing the transformed variable <math>x_t</math>, is to write
<math display="block">y_{t+1}= \alpha - \frac{\beta}{y_t}</math>
where <math>\alpha = (a+d)/c</math>  and <math>\beta = (ad-bc)/c^{2}</math> and where <math>w_t = y_t -d/c</math>.

Further writing  <math>y_t = x_{t+1}/x_t</math> can be shown to yield
<math display="block">x_{t+2} - \alpha x_{t+1} + \beta x_t = 0.</math>

===Second approach===

The above approach is already of general applicability. This following approach<ref>Mitchell, Douglas W., "An analytic Riccati solution for two-target discrete-time control," ''[[Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control]]'' 24, 2000, 615&ndash;622.</ref> gives a first-order difference equation for <math>x_t</math> instead of a second-order one. Let <math>r^2=(d-a)^2+4bc</math>. For the case in which <math>r^2\geqslant0</math>, every term will be real-valued and this method may be convenient to use. Otherwise, the method still works, but complex numbers will appear, and it might be more convenient to attempt a [[Trigonometric functions|trigonometric]] [[ansatz]] instead.  Substituting <math>x_t=1/(\eta+w_t)</math>, which implies <math>w_t=(1-\eta x_t)/x_t</math>, into Equation {{EqNote|2}}, we find that it is always possible to make <math>x_t</math> evolve according to the simple inhomogeneous first-order linear difference equation
<math display="block">x_{t+1} = \left(\frac{d-\eta c}{\eta c+a}\right)\!x_t + \frac{c}{\eta c+a}.</math>
by choosing <math>\eta</math> such that <math>c\eta^2-(d-a)\eta-b=0</math>, and it is clear that this can always be done in either of the two choices <math>\eta_\pm=\frac{d-a\pm r}{2c}</math>, even when <math>r\in\mathbb C</math>

===Third approach===

The equation

<math display="block">w_{t+1} = \frac{aw_t+b}{cw_t+d}</math>

can also be solved by treating it as a special case of the [[Matrix difference equation#Nonlinear matrix difference equations: Riccati equations|more general matrix equation]]

<math display="block">X_{t+1} = -(E+BX_t)(C+AX_t)^{-1},</math>

where all of ''A, B, C, E,'' and ''X'' are ''n'' × ''n'' [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] (in this case ''n'' = 1); the  solution of this is<ref>Martin, C. F., and Ammar, G., "The geometry of the matrix Riccati equation and associated eigenvalue method," in Bittani, Laub, and Willems (eds.), ''The Riccati Equation'', Springer-Verlag, 1991.</ref>

<math display="block">X_t = N_tD_t^{-1}</math>

where

<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix} N_{t} \\ D_{t}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -B & -E \\ A & C \end{pmatrix}^t\begin{pmatrix} X_0\\ I \end{pmatrix}.</math>

==Application==

It was shown in <ref>Balvers, Ronald J., and Mitchell, Douglas W., "Reducing the dimensionality of linear quadratic control problems," ''[[Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control]]'' 31, 2007, 141&ndash;159.</ref> that a dynamic [[matrix Riccati equation]] of the form

<math display="block">H_{t-1} = K +A'H_tA - A'H_tC(C'H_tC)^{-1}C'H_tA,</math>

which can arise in some [[discrete-time]] [[optimal control]] problems, can be solved using the second approach above if the matrix ''C'' has only one more row than column.
